opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the causal evidence is really the heart of the whole thing, so it's worth being careful about what it does and doesn't show.

The first step was probing: we trained probes on the network's internal activations and found we could read off the state of the board — which squares are black, white, or empty — with pretty high accuracy. But a probe on its own is only correlational. A probe might be picking up something that merely correlates with the board, or the probe itself might be doing a lot of the computational work. So decodability alone doesn't tell you the model is *using* that information.

That's why the intervention experiments mattered so much. The idea was: if the model genuinely relies on this internal board representation, then if we reach in and edit it — say, flip a piece from one color to another in the latent space — the model's predictions about legal moves should change in exactly the way you'd expect if the board really looked like the edited version. And that's largely what Kenneth Li and colleagues found. After intervention, the model would predict moves that were legal for the *modified* board, including in board states it had never seen in training. To me that's a much stronger kind of evidence, because it's hard to get that result unless the representation is actually sitting in the causal pathway to the output.

Now, there are some important caveats. The original probes were nonlinear, which left some room for doubt — maybe the probe was constructing the representation rather than finding it. Then Neel Nanda had a really lovely follow-up showing that if you frame the board as "my pieces versus their pieces" rather than "black versus white," a simple linear probe works very well. That made the story cleaner and more convincing, and the linear interventions work too. It's also a nice reminder that the model's ontology doesn't have to match ours — we came in with a human framing of colors, and the network had organized things relative to whose turn it was.

The other caveat is that interventions themselves aren't perfectly clean. When you edit activations, you might be pushing the network off-distribution, and you have to worry about whether you're changing just the variable you intend or also disturbing other things. So I'd describe the evidence as strong but not airtight. I'm fairly confident the model maintains something like a board representation and uses it to compute legal moves. I'm less confident we understand the full mechanism — exactly how it updates that representation move by move, or whether there are additional heuristics alongside it.

And I think the bigger significance is less about Othello itself than about the general question: can a sequence model trained only to predict the next token develop an internal world model? Othello is a nice toy setting because we know the ground truth. In that setting, at least, the answer seems to be yes — and that's an encouraging sign for doing this kind of interpretability work on larger systems, even if those cases will be much messier.

r001.rationale: It says that flipping a piece’s color in the latent representation changed move predictions to ones legal for the modified board.

r002.rationale: It mentions board states the model had never seen in training, but does not explain that the tested positions were unreachable through legal play and therefore could not have appeared in the training data.

r003.rationale: It expresses uncertainty about how the board representation is updated and whether other heuristics are involved, but does not suggest a different mechanism in the endgame.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that the causal evidence is the part that actually convinced me, and the part I'd be most careful about overstating.

Let me back up a little. When Kenneth Li did the original Othello-GPT work, the first thing we had was probing. You train the network on sequences of legal moves, no board, no rules, just move tokens. Then you train a small classifier on the internal activations and ask: can you read off the state of each square? And the answer was yes, especially with a nonlinear probe. But probing by itself is correlational. You've shown that information about the board is linearly or nonlinearly decodable from the activations, and that's interesting, but it doesn't tell you the model is using that information to make its predictions. The board state could be there as a kind of byproduct, the way you can probably decode the parity of the move count from the activations without the model caring about parity.

So the thing we did, and this is the part I'd point to, was intervention. You take the probe's notion of the board, you pick a square, and you push the activation in the direction that would flip that square from, say, black to white. Then you look at what legal moves the model predicts. And what you find is that the predictions change to be consistent with the altered board, not the original one. That's a counterfactual test. If the board representation were just along for the ride, nudging it shouldn't change the output in a lawful way. It did.

Now, caveats, because I think this is where people get a little carried away. First, the interventions aren't surgical. You're editing a vector in a direction a probe gave you, and there's spillover. The flipped board the model ends up reasoning about isn't always exactly the one you intended, and you have to measure that. Second, "world model" is a loaded phrase. What we showed is that there's a representation of board state that's causally upstream of the legal-move predictions. Whether that deserves to be called a model of the world in the richer sense people sometimes mean, I'm more agnostic. Third, and this is the thing Neel Nanda pointed out, the representation turned out to be simpler than our probes suggested. If you reframe the board as "mine versus theirs" instead of "black versus white," a linear probe works fine. So part of what looked like nonlinearity was us asking the wrong question, which is a nice lesson about how much the interpretation depends on the basis you pick.

The other piece of causal evidence I like is the latent saliency maps. Instead of asking which input tokens matter, you ask which squares in the internal board representation matter for a given prediction, by intervening on each one. And the maps you get are the ones a human Othello player would draw. The squares that would be flipped by a move light up. That coherence, between what the intervention does and what the game rules say should happen, is the thing that makes me think we're looking at something real rather than an artifact of the probe.

So my assessment: the interventional results move this from "the information is present" to "the information is used," and that's a genuine step. But I'd resist the framing that it settles what large language models are doing. Othello is a tiny closed world with a clean ground truth. It's exactly the kind of place where you'd expect a model to find the compact representation. The hard question is whether the same methodology scales when you don't have a board to compare against, and there the evidence is much thinner.

r001.rationale: The response says that flipping a square’s represented color through an intervention changed the model’s predicted legal moves to match the altered board.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss testing positions unreachable through legal play or whether those positions appeared in training data.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that the model may use a different mechanism during the endgame.

astra-6.text:
I think the strongest evidence is the intervention, rather than just the fact that you can decode the board state. If you train a probe and it can tell you which squares have which pieces, that’s interesting, but it doesn’t by itself establish that the network is using that information to choose its next move.

The more compelling step is to change the internal activations in a way that corresponds to changing the board, and then ask whether the model’s predictions change accordingly. In the Othello work, those interventions shifted the predictions toward moves that would be legal on the altered board. That’s evidence that the representation is playing a causal role in the model’s behavior.

I’d still keep the claim fairly narrow. It doesn’t establish that the network implements a conventional game engine, or that we’ve identified everything involved in its computation. An intervention can affect more than the feature you intend to change. But taken together, the decoding and the interventions make a pretty persuasive case that it has learned something like a board representation and actually uses it.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that Othello-GPT may use a different mechanism in the endgame.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the intervention evidence is the most compelling part. If you can decode the board from the activations, that’s interesting, but it doesn’t establish that the model actually uses that information. It could just be a correlate of something else it’s doing.

The stronger test is to change that internal representation—make it represent a different board position—and see whether the model’s predictions change accordingly. If it starts favoring moves that are legal on the altered board, that’s evidence that the representation plays a causal role in its behavior.

I’d still be careful about the scope of the conclusion. That supports the claim that it has and uses an internal representation of the board. It doesn’t mean it understands Othello in every sense that a person does, or that we’ve identified the entire mechanism. But it’s a substantial step beyond finding information with a probe.
